This page goes with **Chapter 22, Modulation** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Modulation.html). Read each section there
first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. Everything on this page plays: the examples are written out in four parts
with the Roman numerals under the bass, and a **pivot chord** shows both of its numerals, the old key's above the new one's (the book draws a
bracket). Each section folds from its ▾; the list on the right jumps to any of them.

The examples use the numerals of [Chapter 7](roman-numerals.qmd), the functions of [Chapter 9](progressions.qmd) (T tonic, TP tonic
prolongation, PD pre-dominant, D dominant), and the chromatic chords of Chapters [17](secondary-dominants.qmd),
[19](mode-mixture.qmd) and [20](neapolitan.qmd). [Analysed Scores](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.qmd) has a whole movement full of
modulations to listen to: see [the last section](#moonlight).

## 22.1–22.2 Tonicization or modulation? {#tonicization}

A **modulation** moves the music to a new key and stays there long enough to make it the key: in the book's words, it needs an
eventual **cadence that confirms the new key**, often the full pre-dominant – I⁶₄ – V – I formula. A **tonicization** only borrows
a chord's dominant for a moment (V/V – V, from [Chapter 17](secondary-dominants.qmd)) and the home key never goes away.

Telling them apart is not always easy. A short passage ending with an authentic cadence in a new key could be either, and analysts
disagree. The book's method: find the cadence in the new key, then work backwards to the point where the new key's chords begin; that is
where to look for the pivot.

**Hear the difference.** Both start in C. The first touches G (V/V – V) and comes home; the second goes to G and confirms it with a cadence.

<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="tonicize"></div>
<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="diatonic"></div>

*In the Moonlight:* the B major chord at the start of the second theme (bars 15–19) is read **both ways** by two analysts in
When in Rome: Chen and Su (on Analysed Scores) call it V/iv in B minor, a tonicization; Dmitri Tymoczko calls it V in E minor, a modulation. Nothing ever cadences in E minor.
[See and hear it](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=15-19).

## 22.3 Key relationships {#keys}

**Closely related keys** have key signatures that differ by at most one sharp or flat. Every key has five: its relative major or minor,
and the keys one sharp and one flat away, with their relatives. Any other key is **foreign** (distantly related). Classical
composers most often go from a major key to its dominant and from a minor key to its relative major.

Pick a home key, then click any of its relatives to hear a modulation there (the page finds a pivot chord for it; see 22.4).

<div class="mod-related" data-key="C"></div>

## 22.4 Modulations with diatonic pivot chords {#diatonic-pivot}

A **pivot** (common) chord belongs to both keys: the same root, spelled the same, and the same quality. It is heard first in the old key
and then reheard in the new one. Find candidates by listing the diatonic triads of both keys and matching them.

The book's advice on choosing one:

- a pivot that is **pre-dominant in the new key** (ii, IV, ii°, iv) makes the smoothest move;
- one that is **dominant in the new key** is usually avoided: the change sounds abrupt;
- in the old key the pivot is often **tonic or tonic prolongation** (I, vi, iii).

Choose two keys. Shared chords are highlighted, with each one's function in both keys; **Pivot ▶** writes out and plays a modulation
through that chord, confirmed by a cadence in the new key. Try C to G, C to a minor, c♯ minor to E major (the Moonlight's first
move), and C to F♯ (no common chords).

<div class="mod-pivot" data-from="C" data-to="G"></div>

<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="diatonic"></div>

*In the Moonlight:* bar 7. The F♯ minor chord is iv in c♯ minor and ii in E major, pre-dominant in the new key, followed by
I⁶₄ – V⁷ – I in E.
[See and hear it](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=5-9).
In Tymoczko's reading, the f♯ minor chord in bar 25, i in f♯, becomes iv in c♯ on the way home.

## 22.5 Recognising the new key {#recognise}

Look for **accidentals that keep coming back** and add them to the key signature:

- a new **flat** (or a natural cancelling a sharp) is usually the new key's scale degree 4;
- a new **sharp** (or a natural cancelling a flat) is often its leading tone (scale degree 7): with several, take the one furthest along the
  order of sharps;
- accidentals that are **cancelled again** soon are only tonicizations or chromatic non-chord tones.

*In the Moonlight:* bar 10. The G♯s become G♮ and stay that way: E major has become E minor. Then A♯ appears and keeps coming back,
the leading tone of B minor (bars 12–14).

## 22.6 Modulations with chromatic pivot chords {#chromatic-pivot}

A pivot can be **chromatic** in one or both keys, which lets the music reach keys that share few or no diatonic chords.

**Secondary common chord:** a secondary chord in both keys.

<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="secondary"></div>

**Borrowed common chord:** a chord borrowed from the parallel mode ([Chapter 19](mode-mixture.qmd)) in one key, ordinary in the other.
The book's example is from Beethoven's Op. 110: a borrowed i⁶ in D♭ major, respelled as C♯ minor, becomes vi⁶ in E major.

<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="borrowed"></div>

**Neapolitan common chord:** the [Neapolitan](neapolitan.qmd) can link distantly related keys.

<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="neapolitan"></div>

**Augmented sixth common chord:** an augmented sixth chord reheard as a dominant seventh (or the other way round) is an
*enharmonic* modulation, the subject of the book's next chapter.

*In the Moonlight:* bars 11–14. Tymoczko hears V⁷/V in E minor become V⁷ in B minor, a secondary common chord. (Chen and Su, on Analysed Scores, turn to B minor on a G major chord, III in E minor and VI in B minor.)
[See and hear it](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=11-14).

## 22.7 Modulations without pivot chords {#direct}

**Direct modulation** (also called **phrase modulation**): a phrase ends in one key and the next simply starts in another, with no
pivot. The book's example is Schubert's "Kriegers Ahnung": a half cadence in C minor, then straight into A♭ major.

<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="direct"></div>

**Common-tone modulation:** two chords from different keys are joined by a single shared note, held while the rest moves. It often
links **chromatic mediants**: chords whose roots are a third apart, of the same quality (both major or both minor), that share just
one note. C major and E major share only E.

<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="commontone"></div>

**Sequential modulation:** a passage and its harmony are repeated at a new pitch, and the repetition settles in (or leads to) a new
key. The book cites Mozart's Oboe Concerto, K. 314, III, which moves up by step from C major to D major to E minor.

<div class="mod-ex" data-kind="sequential"></div>

*In the Moonlight:* bars 9–10. E major turns into E minor with no pivot: a direct change of mode.
[See and hear it](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=9-10).

An example in a random key, without its numerals. Listen, look at where the key signature changes and what is happening just before it, and choose. The
numerals appear once you answer.

<div class="mod-quiz"></div>

## In the Moonlight Sonata {#moonlight}

The first movement of Beethoven's Op. 27 No. 2 travels from c♯ minor to E major, E minor, B minor and F♯ minor before coming home, and it
uses almost every kind of modulation on this page. [Analysed Scores](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.qmd) has the whole movement with Chen and Su's
Roman numerals, a strip of the keys they hear, the form part by part, and a table of every modulation with links that play each one.

| Bars | Move | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| [5–9](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=5-9) | c♯ → E | [Diatonic pivot](#diatonic-pivot): iv = ii |
| [9–10](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=9-10) | E → e | [Direct](#direct), a change of mode |
| [11–14](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=11-14) | e → b | [Diatonic pivot](#diatonic-pivot): III = VI (Chen and Su); [secondary common chord](#chromatic-pivot) (Tymoczko) |
| [15–19](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=15-19) | B major: b or e? | [Tonicization or modulation](#tonicization) |
| [19–23](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=19-23) | → f♯ | Through the new key's own dominant, confirmed by a cadence |
| [23–27](analysed-scores/beethoven-moonlight-1.html?piece=beethoven-moonlight-1&bars=23-27) | f♯ → c♯ | [Diatonic pivot](#diatonic-pivot): i = iv (Tymoczko) |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For teachers

- **The examples are this site's**, not the book's (the book's are recordings and score images), each written in four parts: the
  bass, and three upper voices that move as little as possible from chord to chord. They are not checked for every
  part-writing rule. The quiz transposes them to any key that needs no double sharps or flats and no more than six sharps or flats.
- **Common chords** are the diatonic triads only. Minor keys list i ii° III iv v V VI VII vii° (both forms of the dominant
  and of the 7th degree), so a chord made from the natural minor counts. A pivot is chosen automatically for the closely related key
  buttons: pre-dominant in the new key if possible, never dominant there.
- **Functions** follow Chapter 9: I and i are T; vi, VI, iii and III are TP; IV, iv, ii and ii° are PD; V, v, vii° and VII are D.
  The book treats VII in minor and iii in major more carefully than this table does.
- **The Moonlight links** open Analysed Scores with the bars lit; press ▶ there (or the bar links in its modulation table) to hear them.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
